fr.R: Otniel, fils de Kenaz, le frère de Caleb, a pris la ville. Alors Caleb lui a donné sa fille Aksa en mariage.

vi.L: Ốt-ni-ên con trai Kê-na, em của Ca-lép, chiếm được nó; và ông gả Ạc-sa, con gái mình, cho người ấy làm vợ.
vi.B: Ốt-ni-ên con trai Kê-na, em của Ca-lép, chiếm được thành ấy, nên Ca-lép gả con gái mình là Ạc-sa cho người ấy làm vợ.
vi.R: Ốt-ni-ên con trai Kê-na, em của Ca-lép, chiếm được thành ấy. Vì thế Ca-lép gả con gái mình là Ạc-sa cho người ấy làm vợ.

ko.L: 그리고 갈렙의 형제 그나스의 아들 옷니엘이 그것을 차지하였다. 그리고 그가 그에게 자기 딸 악사를 아내로 주었다.
ko.B: 갈렙의 아우 그나스의 아들 옷니엘이 그 성읍을 차지하였다. 그래서 갈렙은 자기 딸 악사를 그에게 아내로 주었다.
ko.R: 갈렙의 아우 그나스의 아들 옷니엘이 그 성읍을 차지하였다. 그래서 갈렙은 자기 딸 악사를 옷니엘의 아내로 주었다.

pt.L: E Otniel, filho de Quenaz, irmão de Calebe, a tomou; e ele lhe deu Acsa, sua filha, por mulher.
pt.B: Otniel, filho de Quenaz, irmão de Calebe, a conquistou, e Calebe lhe deu a sua filha Acsa como esposa.
pt.R: Otniel, filho de Quenaz, irmão de Calebe, conquistou a cidade. Então Calebe lhe deu a sua filha Acsa para ser a esposa dele.

decisions.choice: the brother of Caleb: most likely Othniel, possibly Kenaz
alternatives: Othniel son of Kenaz, who was Caleb's brother
Othniel, son of Caleb's brother Kenaz
decisions.reason: The words could describe either Othniel or his father Kenaz. Judges 1:13 and 3:9 call Othniel "Caleb's younger brother", so he is probably meant; "brother" may also mean a close relative of the same clan, since Caleb is called "the Kenizzite" (14:6). Every level keeps the Hebrew's order so either reading remains possible.

decisions.choice: Othniel: later the first of the judges
decisions.reason: Othniel later rescued Israel from the king of Aram-naharaim and led it for forty years (Judges 3:9-11).

decisions.choice: Caleb gave
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Caleb as the one who gave, since "he" could be read as Othniel.

decisions.choice: "Otoniel"; "Acsa"; "Quenaz"
decisions.reason: As the terms note for Joshua, Judges and Ruth sets, Othniel is "Otoniel", the usual Spanish form, which returns in Judges 1 and 3; Achsah and Kenaz likewise in their usual Spanish forms.

decisions.choice: "em của Ca-lép": the younger brother
decisions.reason: Vietnamese must say whether a brother is older or younger. Othniel belongs to the next generation of leaders (Judges 3:9), so he is taken as the younger; whether "brother" here is Othniel or Kenaz is a question of meaning the English decisions discuss.

decisions.choice: "형제" (L); "아우" (B, R) for "the brother of Caleb"
decisions.reason: Korean must say whether a brother is older or younger. Literal keeps the open word "형제"; Balanced and Readable say "아우", since Caleb was already eighty-five (14:10) and Othniel lived on to be Israel's first judge. Meaning decision m1 notes that "Caleb's brother" may describe Kenaz instead; Korean keeps the Hebrew order and leaves that open as the English does.

decisions.choice: Otniel, filho de Quenaz, irmão de Calebe (every level)
alternatives: Otniel, filho de Quenaz, que era irmão de Calebe
decisions.reason: For the whole book and Judges 1:13 and 3:9: "Otniel" is the usual Brazilian form, and "Quenaz" the form of Genesis 36:11 in Portuguese. Every level keeps "irmão de Calebe" right after "filho de Quenaz", as the English does, so that it can describe either man (m1); a relative clause would decide for Othniel.

source.text: וַיְהִ֣י בְּבוֹאָ֗הּ וַתְּסִיתֵ֨הוּ֙ לִשְׁא֤וֹל מֵֽאֵת־אָבִ֨יהָ֙ שָׂדֶ֔ה וַתִּצְנַ֖ח מֵעַ֣ל הַחֲמ֑וֹר וַיֹּֽאמֶר־לָ֥הּ כָּלֵ֖ב מַה־לָּֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, when she came, and she urged him to ask from her father a field; and she got down from on the donkey, and said to her Caleb, What to you?

en.L: And it happened, when she came, that she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she got down from the donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What [do] you [want]?"
en.B: When she came to Othniel, she urged him to ask her father for a field. As she got down from her donkey, Caleb asked her, "What do you want?"
en.R: When Achsah came to be Othniel's wife, she urged him to ask her father for a field. Then she got down from her donkey, and Caleb asked her, "What can I do for you?"

sw.L: Na ikawa, alipokuja, akamhimiza amwombe baba yake shamba. Naye akashuka kutoka juu ya punda, na Kalebu akamwambia, "Wewe [unataka] nini?"
sw.B: Alipokuja kwa Othnieli, alimhimiza amwombe baba yake shamba. Aliposhuka kutoka juu ya punda wake, Kalebu akamwuliza, "Unataka nini?"
sw.R: Aksa alipokuja kuwa mke wa Othnieli, alimhimiza amwombe baba yake shamba. Kisha akashuka kutoka juu ya punda wake, na Kalebu akamwuliza, "Nikufanyie nini?"

es.L: Y sucedió que, cuando ella llegó, lo instó a pedir a su padre un campo. Y ella se bajó del asno, y Caleb le dijo: «¿Qué [quieres]?».

es.R: Cuando Acsa llegó para ser la esposa de Otoniel, lo animó a pedirle un campo a su padre. Luego ella se bajó del asno, y Caleb le preguntó: «¿Qué puedo hacer por ti?».

decisions.choice: when she came: when she came to her husband as a bride
decisions.reason: The coming is her arrival at Othniel's home at the marriage. Her request may belong to the gift a father gave with his daughter at her marriage.

decisions.choice: she urged him: Achsah urged Othniel
alternatives: he urged her to ask her father for a field
decisions.reason: The Hebrew here reads "she urged him". The ancient Greek translation, here and in Judges 1:14, reads "he urged her", so that Othniel prompts Achsah to ask. The Hebrew is followed, since in verse 19 Achsah is the one who speaks. This description of the manuscripts is from general knowledge; reviewers should check it against a critical edition.

decisions.choice: she got down: slipped down quickly from the donkey
alternatives: she called out from the donkey
decisions.reason: The verb is rare (Judges 1:14; 4:21). It seems to mean a quick downward movement; getting down before an older man showed respect before a request (Genesis 24:64; 1 Samuel 25:23). Some take it to mean that she clapped her hands or called out.

decisions.choice: what to you?: what do you want?
decisions.reason: The short question asks what a person wishes or needs, as in Judges 1:14 and 1 Kings 1:16.

decisions.choice: to Othniel (B); Achsah came to be Othniel's wife; urged him (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the people the pronouns point to, and Readable says what her coming was (m1).

decisions.choice: What can I do for you?
decisions.reason: Readable gives the idiom as a father's kind offer of help; Literal and Balanced keep a plain question.

decisions.choice: Caleb and his daughter speak as "cha" and "con"
decisions.reason: As the Genesis terms note sets for parent and child.

decisions.choice: Caleb speaks to his daughter in the plain style (해라체: "원하느냐", "해 주랴"); she answers in the polite style (해요체)
decisions.reason: The terms note for Genesis: a parent speaks to a child in the plain style, and a child answers a parent politely. Achsah's request is warm and direct, so 해요체 ("주세요") fits her better than the formal 합쇼체.

decisions.reason: The rare verb seems to mean a quick movement down (m3); Literal says "desceu depressa", and Balanced and Readable say "desceu", as the English does. Caleb speaks to his daughter with "você", as people speak to one another (docs/portuguese-style.md, section 4).

es.L: Y ella dijo: «Dame una bendición; ya que me has dado la tierra del Néguev, dame también manantiales de agua». Y él le dio los manantiales de arriba y los manantiales de abajo.

es.R: Ella respondió: «Por favor, hazme un regalo. Me has dado tierra en el sur seco, así que dame también algunos manantiales de agua». Y Caleb le dio los manantiales de arriba y los de abajo.

decisions.reason: Achsah asks her father for a gift, and a Brazilian daughter making a request of her father addresses him with "o senhor", with the imperative that goes with it, "Dê-me" (docs/portuguese-style.md, section 4); "tu" is kept for speech to God. Judges 1:15 should keep the same.

decisions.choice: uma bênção (L), um presente (B, R); fontes de água; as fontes superiores e as fontes inferiores (L), as fontes de cima e as fontes de baixo (B, R)
alternatives: as fontes altas e as fontes baixas
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "bênção", which Portuguese can also say of a gift given in goodwill (m1); Balanced and Readable say "presente". decisions.choice: the town list in four regions
decisions.reason: Judah's towns are listed by the regions of its land: the Negev in the south (verses 21-32), the Shephelah or low hills in the west (verses 33-47), the hill country (verses 48-60) and the wilderness by the Dead Sea (verses 61-62). Within each region the towns are counted in groups, and each group closes with its total.

decisions.choice: Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur: towns of the far south
decisions.reason: Kabzeel was the home of Benaiah, one of David's warriors (2 Samuel 23:20). The sites of all three are not known for certain.

decisions.choice: the town names in their usual Spanish forms (Cabseel, Edar, Jagur ...), every one kept
decisions.reason: As the terms note asks for the lists of names in Joshua 13-21: every name is kept, in the form Spanish Bibles have long used, with Spanish spelling (c and qu for k, s for sh) and accents where Spanish writes them (Hebrón, Ecrón, Bet-semes). Literal keeps the Hebrew "and" between names; Balanced and Readable use commas, as the English does.

decisions.choice: "villes" at every level, for the English "cities" (Literal) and "towns" (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: French "ville" covers both a city and a small town, and "bourg" or "localité" would sound technical in a list. One word at every level keeps the lists simple; the villages around them are "villages".

decisions.choice: the town names of verses 21-62 in their usual Brazilian forms; rare ones spelled by pattern
decisions.reason: For this chapter. Names the Bible tells more of keep their Portuguese forms (Berseba, Hormá, Ziclague, Laquis, Eglom, Jarmute, Adulão, Maquedá, Libna, Hebrom, Gósen, Carmelo, Jezreel, En-Gedi; Mispe as 11:8 for the Mizpeh of verse 38). Many others are named only here, and no Portuguese form is settled for them: Cabzeel, Éder, Jagur, Quiná, Itnã, Bealote, Queriote-Hezrom, Biziotiá, Iim, Quesil, Silim, Enã, Aditaim, Gederotaim, Zenã, Dileã, Bozcate, Cabom, Laamás, Quitlis, Iftá, Nezibe, Daná, Quiriate-Sana, Esã, Janum, Afeca, Hunta, Zior, Jocdeão, Maarate, Midim, Secacá, Nibsã. They are written by the pattern of the other names ("qu" for k and ch before e and i, "s" for sh, a final -on "-om" and -an "-ã", -oth "-ote", a stressed final -ah "-á", "Bete-", "Hazar-", "Quiriate-" and "En-" joined with a hyphen) and are uncertain. "Caim" (verse 57) has the form of Cain's name, as the Hebrew does; "Estemo" (verse 50) is kept apart from "Estemoa" (21:14), as the English keeps Eshtemoh and Eshtemoa.

decisions.choice: their villages: the unwalled settlements around the towns
decisions.reason: The word means open settlements without walls, belonging to a walled town nearby (Leviticus 25:31). Each count in the list numbers the towns; the villages are added without a number.

decisions.choice: twenty-nine: fewer than the names listed
decisions.reason: Verses 21-32 name about thirty-six places, but the total is twenty-nine. The reason is not known. Some names may belong together as one town (Ain and Rimmon may be En-rimmon, Nehemiah 11:29), some may be villages rather than towns, and the list may have been brought up to date after the total was written, when towns were given to Simeon (19:1-9).

decisions.choice: Lebaoth, Shilhim
decisions.reason: Lebaoth is probably the Beth-lebaoth of 19:6. Shilhim may be the Sharuhen of the same verse.

decisions.choice: in all, twenty-nine cities (L), towns (B, R), and their villages
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "cities"; Balanced and Readable say "towns" (verse 9). Every group in the list closes with the same words. Readable says "the villages around them" to show that the villages belonged to the towns (m1).

decisions.choice: "miji ... na vijiji vyake" at every level

decisions.choice: the Greek adds a group of eleven towns after this verse
alternatives: add the eleven towns of the Greek text
decisions.reason: After "six towns and their villages" the ancient Greek translation has a further group not in the Hebrew: Tekoa, Ephrathah (that is, Bethlehem), Peor, Etam, Kulon, Tatam, Sores, Karem, Gallim, Bether and Manocho, "eleven cities and their villages". These are towns of the hill country around Bethlehem, which the Hebrew list does not name at all. The lines may have dropped out of the Hebrew when a copyist's eye passed from one "and their villages" to the next, or they may have been added in the Greek. The Hebrew text is followed. This account is from general knowledge, and the spellings of the Greek names vary between manuscripts; reviewers should check it against a critical edition.

decisions.choice: the Jebusites in Jerusalem: a city not taken
decisions.reason: Jerusalem lay on the border with Benjamin (verse 8; 18:16, 28), and neither tribe took it (Judges 1:21). Judges 1:8 tells of Judah burning part of it, but the Jebusites kept their stronghold until David captured it (2 Samuel 5:6-9).

decisions.choice: to this day: up to the time of writing
decisions.reason: The phrase speaks from the writer's own time. The Jebusites were still living in Jerusalem, among the people of Judah, in the writer's day.

decisions.choice: they were able: the reading the scribes marked
decisions.reason: The written consonants and the reading the scribes marked differ only in the form of the verb "were able"; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: And the Jebusites ... — the children of Judah were not able
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts the Jebusites first for emphasis and then starts the sentence again. Literal shows this with a dash; Balanced and Readable make one sentence.

decisions.choice: But (B, R); So (R)
decisions.reason: The opening "and" sets this against the list of towns Judah received, so Balanced and Readable say "But". Readable makes the result clear with "So".

decisions.choice: até este dia (L); até hoje (B, R); habitam, vivem (present)
decisions.reason: The writer speaks from his own day (m2), so the phrase keeps the wording 4:9 sets for the whole book, "até este dia" at Literal and "até hoje" at Balanced and Readable, and the verb is in the present, as the English says "have lived" and "live". "Os jebuseus" is the form of 3:10.
